title: What the Water Was Holding
logline: A reservoir built across a mountain valley drowned dozens of villages and their temples, and in a hard dry year the water falls far enough that the foundations, the wells and the steps of one of them stand up out of the mud again, exactly where they always were.
human_question: If something can be out of sight for thirty years and come back unchanged, what does it mean to say it has gone?

place.what_kind_of_place: A large hydroelectric reservoir filling a steep mountain valley, made by damming a river some decades ago. Filling it put a long list of villages, estates and old temples under water, and their people were moved to new settlements on the slopes above the shoreline. For most of the reservoir's life the water sits high and the valley reads as a lake with wooded ridges falling into it. In a severe dry year the level drops tens of metres, and a wide belt of cracked, pale, dead ground appears between the trees and the water, with the tops of buildings standing in it.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: A reservoir at low water is one of the strangest landscapes anywhere: a lake with a bathtub ring, and below the ring a country nobody has walked on since the year it was flooded. From the air the shoreline reads as a tide line drawn round a whole valley, and inside it the geometry of a settlement comes back as pale rectangles in grey silt, with a road going down into the water and not coming out. At ground level the surfaces are the story. Plaster that has been under water for decades is still plaster. Steps still have their edges. A brick wall still has its courses. Nothing has been worn away; it has only been out of view.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Only the water, and only partly on the weather's terms. The level falls through a dry spell or a hard generating season, holds for a few weeks, and the first heavy rain in the catchment takes the whole thing back in days. The exposure is not annual and cannot be forecast, but it is commoner than the travel writing says: the upper part of the temple has been photographed standing clear of the water in February, April, May and even August, in wet years as well as dry ones, because the level is set by generation and by downstream irrigation as much as by rainfall - the reservoir's working range is nearly forty metres. What is genuinely rare is a fall deep enough to put the ground around the building in air rather than shallows. Within a single day the light changes the exposed ground completely, from white glare at noon to a long raking shadow across every threshold at the end of the afternoon.
place.when_it_looks_best: At the deepest point of a drawdown, whenever one comes. In the dated record that has most often meant April, but exposures are also on record in February, May and August, and the meteorological literature disagrees with itself about which month the reservoir is lowest, so the film waits on a reading rather than a calendar. Early morning for mist on the remaining water and for the ridges above the tide line; the last hour of light for the exposed masonry, when low sun makes every step and every wall base throw a shadow and the plan of the place becomes readable from the air.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A landscape film about a lake that goes down. It has a full shape on its own: a wooded valley with a still sheet of water in it, then a widening band of pale cracked ground, then a settlement standing up out of the silt, then the same frames again with the water back over them. The textures alone carry it, mud that dries into plates, a wall that has kept its corners, a road that walks into the water. Anyone who never hears a word of it gets a complete piece with a fall, a revelation and a closing over.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same drawdown becomes the sources' own image standing in a real valley. One of the two texts explains a whole class of unwholesome states as a great mass of water going over fields, gardens and villages, and another explains a different class as things that lie hidden, holding on, with the strength to rise again whenever a suitable occasion turns up. Here both are one place, and neither has to be argued: a valley genuinely under a flood, and a town that was never destroyed, only covered. The voice reads the water and the mud, never anybody's face, and makes no claim at all about what is in anyone's mind.

sequence.on_screen: Drone, very high, early morning. A long reservoir filling a steep valley, mist lying on it, wooded ridges going down into it on both sides. Nothing unusual at all.
sequence.voice: This valley had villages in it, and tea land, and a long list of old temples. Then a dam was finished downstream and the river was asked to stop. Everything below a certain line went under and the people who lived there were moved uphill. That was more than a working lifetime ago.

sequence.on_screen: The same water at the surface: flat, grey-green, giving nothing back. A boat wake crossing it and closing again.
sequence.voice: One of the old texts has a word for a whole family of these states, and its image for them is water. Not a pool: a current. Something that falls into a river is taken by the eddy and carried to the floor of the sea. The other text puts it as a flood going over fields, gardens and villages [C074-P:L112–L114; C074-M:L27–L31]. That is a simile everywhere else. Here it is the survey map.

sequence.on_screen: A dry season, weeks in. Aerial: the water has pulled back and a wide pale band of cracked silt now rings the whole valley, with the green stopping at a level line far above it.
sequence.voice: A bad dry year takes the level down a long way. What comes out from under it is not new ground. It is old ground, that has been there the entire time, at the same elevation, in the same order.

sequence.on_screen: Walking speed across the exposed bed: dried mud in plates, bleached tree stumps still rooted where they grew, a metalled road running down the slope and continuing straight into the water.
sequence.voice: The texts describe some of these states as lying hidden, not showing themselves, keeping hold of the stream of mind until they are cut, and having the strength to come up again whenever a suitable occasion is found [C074-P:L474]. The same texts set out three stages: lying low, rising into the mind, and moving the body and the voice [C074-P:L486–L498; C074-M:L73–L79]. Only the last one can be photographed.

sequence.on_screen: The settlement itself. Foundations in a grid, doorsteps, a well with its rim intact, a temple platform with its statues still in place, silt to the ankles. Late low sun: every edge throws a shadow.
sequence.voice: None of this was destroyed. It was covered. The steps still have their edges. The wall still has its courses. Thirty years of being out of sight did not take one thing away from it, and the texts are blunt about what follows from that: holding something down is not the same as being done with it. The one is a level. The other is a change in the ground.

sequence.on_screen: Back on the water at dusk, once it has begun to rise again. Flat light, no wind, an unbroken grey surface. Nothing visible below it.
sequence.voice: The other text in this group says that when the mind is darkened it cannot take a matter as it really is [C008-M:L3], and it describes a mind that cannot come to a decision about the thing in front of it [C008-P:L34]. It also says something easy to miss: a mind in that state feels neither good nor bad, because you cannot like or dislike what you have not got hold of [C008-P:L30]. A flat surface is not a calm one. It is a surface you cannot see through.

sequence.on_screen: After the first heavy rain in the catchment. The same aerial as beat 3, days later: the pale band gone, the water back at the tree line, the valley reading again as an ordinary lake.
sequence.voice: It takes one wet week to put it all back. The film has no opinion about anybody who lived here and makes no claim about anybody's mind; a camera cannot see that and this one does not pretend to. It only shows the arrangement. Nothing under there has changed. The level has.

concept_merge.why_together: Read fresh, C074 does almost all the work and does it twice over. Its flood image is not decoration here: the texts explain that family of states as a current that takes whatever falls in down to the sea floor, and the second source as a great mass of water going over fields, gardens and villages [C074-P:L112–L114; C074-M:L27–L31], which is a literal description of what was done to this valley. Its latent tendencies then supply the second half: states that lie hidden and keep the strength to rise whenever a suitable occasion appears [C074-P:L474], set out in three stages of which only the last is visible in body or speech [C074-P:L486–L498; C074-M:L73–L79]. C008 supplies the group's question and the reason the film has anything to do with not-seeing at all: delusion is described as what darkens the mind so a matter cannot be known as it is [C008-M:L3], and the full reservoir is exactly that, a surface that withholds. Put on one drawdown, the flood, the thing lying low and the surface that hides it are the same body of water at three different levels.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That hiddenness is not absence, and that finding this out is quiet rather than dramatic. C074 alone would be a diagram with two similes in it. C008 alone would be a mood over grey water. Together they make the one point the place can prove without asking anyone to believe anything: what was covered is still the size and shape it was, in the same position, and the only thing that ever changed was how much was standing over it. The pairing also blocks the sentimental ending, because the return of the ruins is not a recovery. It is a level, and the level goes back up.

concept_links.why: Two of the compendium's nine lists land on this place directly. The floods are explained as a current that drags whatever falls into the river down to the floor of the sea, and by the second source as a great water going over fields, gardens and villages, with escape from it very hard [C074-P:L112–L114; C074-M:L27–L31]. The latent tendencies are explained as unwholesome states that keep hold of the mind-stream unseen until path-knowledge cuts them, with the power to arise again whenever a suitable object is met [C074-P:L474], and both books set out the three stages of lying low, surfacing in the mind, and breaking out into act and speech [C074-P:L486–L498; C074-M:L73–L79]. The digest's limits are load-bearing and are honoured on screen. Abandonment is staged and technical, not a lifestyle decision, so the returning water is not offered as relapse and the drawdown is not offered as release: beat 5 says only that suppression and uprooting are different. 'Your mind is pure underneath' does not follow from anything here and is never implied by the image of clean ground under water. The stakes in the source are not stress or wellbeing, so no well-being language is used. And the warnings about rites and rituals concern views held as the path to liberation and cannot be turned on anyone's practice, which matters because one of the exposed buildings is a temple that people come to when it appears.

Delusion is described as the quality that darkens the mind so that a matter cannot be known as it really is, present in all unwholesome minds [C008-M:L3]; the doubt built on it is a mind unable to reach a decision about its object [C008-P:L34]. A full reservoir is a surface that gives no information about what is under it, which is what this film can actually observe. The digest's two guards are kept. The harmful doubt it means is restricted to eight specifically religious matters and is separated explicitly from ordinary not-knowing about something one cannot yet investigate [C008-P:L36], so the film asserts nothing about which kind of not-seeing is in play; it describes water. And the neutral feeling that comes with these states is a dull greyness from failing to grasp the object, not equanimity [C008-P:L30], which is why beat 6 refuses to read the flat evening surface as peace.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That something out of sight is not the same as something gone. A settlement can be under water for thirty years and come back with its steps, its walls and its street plan intact, because nothing was ever taken away from it. The texts describe some states of mind in exactly those terms, and they are careful to add that holding a thing down and being finished with it are not the same operation.
what_must_be_real: The drought, the drawdown and the reservoir. The exposure is filmed on whatever weeks it actually happens and is never simulated, composited or graded into existence, and the water level is never described as lower or higher than it was. Nobody who was moved out of the valley is interviewed, filmed, identified, traced or asked about on the film's behalf - not at the site, not in the resettlement areas, not through anybody else; that rule is absolute and no footage depends on breaking it. No former resident is brought to the site for the camera, asked to point out a house, asked to remember on cue, or filmed in grief; if people come of their own accord the film treats them as it treats anyone in a public place, and a resettlement history that is still painful is not flattened into a story with a villain or offered as an illustration of anything. No object is moved, cleaned, uncovered, lifted or arranged on the exposed ground, and anything at the temple is left exactly as found. If the bed is not safe to walk, it is filmed from the air only.
position_hint: middle, sitting early in the group: it makes the group's plainest statement, that what is covered has not gone, and it gives the viewer a physical fact to hold before the harder films about direction and speed. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Narrating the displacement at all beyond the plain record. People were moved out of these villages and many of them are alive. The film states once what the scheme did - the volumes, the dates, the counted families - and adjudicates nothing. It does not present the move as loss, as injustice, as sacrifice for the nation or as progress; C061 bars legacy and remembrance framing outright, so there is no elegy, no lament, no 'what they left behind', and no music supplying a grief the narration refuses. Nobody who was moved is interviewed, filmed, identified or sought out, and nobody is sent looking for them; if people are present at the drawdown they are a crowd or they are not in the film.
Making the reappearance uncanny, eerie or ghostly. It is a structure in a drawdown zone. The honest description is that it stands exactly where it always was, and the film has no other.

Treating the exposed building, or the large stupa above the right bank, as a memorial. One is a temple in a drawdown zone and the other is a stupa raised in connection with the scheme; neither is used to make the film mourn.

Presenting any person on screen, or their memory, or their disagreement, as an instance of a defilement or as confusion. The sources describe moments of mind, and a camera cannot show which factor is present.

Using the digest's warnings about rites and rituals against the people who come to the exposed temple. Those warnings concern views taken as the path to liberation and cannot be turned on anyone's practice.
Implying that the clean ground under the water shows a pure mind underneath. The digest rules that reading out explicitly.
Reading the flat grey surface as calm or the drawdown as release; the digest is explicit that the neutral feeling in these states is not equanimity, and that suppression is not uprooting.
Self-help framing. The stakes in the source are not stress, wellbeing or letting go of baggage.
Exposed reservoir ground that looks solid and is not, plus dam-authority restrictions and drone rules over infrastructure.

Reading the figures as a verdict. The counts of villages, temples, hectares and families disagree between sources, partly because no pre-evacuation baseline was ever taken, and the film says so rather than picking the largest number.
drop_if: No drawdown deep enough to expose the remains occurs during the development window, and the film would have to be built from archive.
Access to the exposed bed cannot be had safely or lawfully.
It can only be made by bringing former residents back to the site for the camera.

connections.note: A surface that hides what is under it, and a surface that hides which way to go.
The group opens on something covered by water and closes on something covered by cloud.

selection.reason: The only idea in the group that shows a thing lying hidden and returning unchanged when conditions change, with the sources' own flood image standing in the actual landscape.

review.note: Rewritten 2026-09-22 into the footage-led shape. Situation block replaced by place, two_layers and a seven-beat sequence; both digests re-read from scratch and the film rebuilt around C074's own flood simile and its account of what lies low, with C008 demoted to the surface that withholds. Per the group brief the film was moved off returning residents entirely and onto the water and the ground, and a proposed location was added. Research pass 2026-09-25: a historical_thread was added to suggested_location - the national development programme the dam belongs to, the dam's and reservoir's own figures from the electricity authority's station data, what was submerged with the counts held apart where the sources disagree, the resettlement figures from the 1988-90 evacuees study, the stupa raised in connection with the submergence, the temple's own record and the dated history of its reappearances. The body of the film is unchanged, so this does not reset the verdict. Outside suggested_location, only facts moved: place.what_moves_or_changes and place.when_it_looks_best were corrected because the claim that the ruins had surfaced only a handful of times in thirty years, and only in March and April, is contradicted by dated photographs and by a February 2026 exposure that followed a spill rather than a drought; best_time, access and unknowns were rewritten around that; a risks entry and a what_must_be_real line now state the displacement floor and the absolute no-interview rule explicitly; four verified images were added and the coordinates replaced with the published ones for the temple. The logline, two_layers, sequence and concept_merge were not touched.

suggested_location.name: Kadadora Viharaya and the drawdown zone of the Kotmale Reservoir

also_known_as.name: Pratibimbarama
also_known_as.meaning: the monastery of the reflection; the older name the site is believed to carry

suggested_location.region: The Kotmale valley, Nuwara Eliya district, central highlands, upstream of the Kotmale dam and reached from the Gampola side
suggested_location.why_here: It puts the concept and the spectacle in one frame and nowhere else does. Filling this reservoir between November 1984 and early 1985 put a long list of villages, tea estates and old temples under water — the figures in circulation are 57 villages, 14 estates and around 54 temples and shrines — so the second source's image for the floods, a great mass of water going over fields, gardens and villages, is not a simile here but the recorded engineering history of the valley, with a volume, a top water level and a minimum operating level attached to it. And the structure that comes back is not a ruin that was ruined: it is a building that was left where it stood and covered, so when the level falls it stands at exactly the elevation it always occupied. That is the shape the texts give to something that lies low and shows itself when conditions suit, and it can be filmed rather than argued. The best image the place produces, a temple image house and a seated Buddha figure standing in grey silt below a tide line drawn round a whole valley, is also the clearest statement of the concept.

historical_thread.story:
The Kotmale Oya is the largest right-bank tributary of the Mahaweli Ganga, and the valley it runs through was the most upstream of the headworks sites of the Accelerated Mahaweli Development Programme. A dam here was first proposed in 1961; investigations ran from 1964 to 1968 and a feasibility study from 1973 to 1976, the latter by Water Power Development Consultancy Services of India. Construction began in 1979 — accounts give February, August and September of that year. The Kotmale Dam is an embankment dam 87 m high with three spillways; its crest is given as 520 m in some accounts and 600 m in others. Filling of the reservoir began in November 1984, ahead of a contractual completion date of 22 August 1985; one Sinhala account gives 27 February 1985 as the day the gates were closed, the dam was ceremonially completed in February 1985, and generation began in 1985. Water is carried 7.2 km underground to a power station at Atabage, where three vertical Francis units of 67 MW each give an installed capacity of 201 MW and an expected 450 GWh a year, the second largest hydroelectric station in the country. The Ceylon Electricity Board's own station data give the reservoir a maximum level of 703 m above mean sea level and a minimum operating level of 665 m, a gross storage of 174 million cubic metres to top water level and a usable volume of 154 million, on a catchment of 544 km2. The surface at normal top water level is 6.5 km2, the maximum depth 90 m, the mean depth 26.8 m and the shoreline 45 km. The reservoir was renamed the Gamini Dissanayaka Reservoir on 11 April 2003. The project began as an agreement between two private Swedish contractors and the Sri Lankan government; the Swedish International Development Authority was brought in during construction because of financial constraints, which, in the words of one of its own consultants, meant in effect taking over the implementation of a project designed by others.

What the filling covered is recorded in round figures that do not agree. The most widely repeated set is 57 villages, 14 tea estates and around 54 old temples and shrines; the article on the commemorative stupa says over 50 temples; one Sri Lankan site says about 50; a Sinhala feature gives over 50 villages and 18 temples. For land, the figure usually given is nearly 4,000 ha of the upper catchment, including 600 ha of paddy, while the reservoir's own coverage is given as 2,270 ha across the Kandy and Nuwara Eliya districts. Named submerged religious sites include the Kadadora Vihara, the Thispane Vihara, the Othalawa Vihara, the Medagoda Vihara, the Morape Devalaya and a Pattini Devalaya.

The people were moved. The clearest published account of the numbers comes from the Kotmale Evacuees Study, commissioned by SIDA and begun in the spring of 1988, reported on by Lars T. Soeftestad of the Development Studies Unit at the Department of Social Anthropology, University of Stockholm, in Bistandsantropologen no. 15, pp 22-32, June 1990. It records 3,056 families already relocated: 1,334 who took relocation higher up the hillsides inside the Kotmale valley itself, and 1,722 who moved downstream and out of Kotmale, mostly into the large settlement schemes of the lower Mahaweli in the dry zone. A further 905 families were listed for evacuation upstream, making 3,961 in all. Evacuation had two causes: inundation of land or houses, and subsequent landslides. Other figures circulate — around 3,400 families including some 900 from landslide-prone ground, and approximately 3,000 in one popular account. The study states flatly that no data on the situation before evacuation existed, which is why it had to be designed as an impact analysis rather than an evaluation; it also records that the official undertaking of 0.8 ha per family for those who stayed in the valley was not kept, actual allotments running between 0.2 and 0.8 ha. A later study by Jagath Manatunge and Naruhiko Takesada, in the International Journal of Water Resources Development 29(1), 2013, pp 87-100, revisited resettlers at eight sites in Mahaweli Systems B, C and H. That literature is recorded here because it is the official and scholarly record of what the scheme did. It is not the film's subject, and the people in it are not approached.

One thing was built in connection with the submergence. The Kotmale Mahaweli Maha Seya, a stupa 88 m high standing at about 950 m above sea level on the high ground over the right bank, came from a proposal by Gamini Dissanayake, then Minister of Mahaweli Development, in connection with the submerged temples and the people who lost property. Its structural design was by Vidya Jyothi Dr A. N. S. Kulasinghe, who died before it was finished. President J. R. Jayewardene laid the foundation stone on 20 March 1983; the work was completed and the stupa opened by President Maithripala Sirisena and Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe on 20 June 2016, and it is described as second in height to the Ruwanwelisaya at Anuradhapura.

The building that reappears is the Kadadora Sri Priyabimbaramaya Viharaya, in Kadadora in the Nuwara Eliya district, recorded at 7.06083 N, 80.59722 E. Some accounts identify the site with an older temple called Pratibimbarama, the monastery of the reflection, and say its history runs back several centuries; others say plainly that the building submerged in the 1980s was put up by the villagers in the early twentieth century. The described plan is an image house with a garbhagriha holding the principal Buddha figure, with smaller rooms and gathering space round it, and wall paintings of scenes from the Buddha's life and the Jataka stories. The resident monks are said to have left for higher ground around 1979. What has been photographed standing out of the water is the image house and its walls, a seated Buddha figure, carved stone work including a makara torana at the entrance, a bodhigharaya wall and a flower altar, with paintings faintly traceable on the remaining plaster. Across the water the Thispane Vihara also surfaces, of which only foundation walls are left, and further east a gopuram tower of a former Hindu temple can come out of the reservoir.

The reappearances are datable. The ruins are reported to have come back around 2009, after roughly thirty years, and the Daily News carried a report of ruins emerging on 30 March 2016. Photographs on Wikimedia Commons carry camera dates of 23 April 2016, 3 August 2017, 15-19 April 2019 and 5 May 2020. Sinhala press reports appeared in April 2019 and April 2021. On 5 February 2026 a Sinhala broadcaster reported the statues visible again, the level having fallen fast after the rains of Cyclone Ditwah at the end of November 2025 — the same reservoir had been spilling in early December 2025. So the claim, common in travel writing, that the site has surfaced only three or four times in more than thirty years is contradicted by the dated pictures, and the exposures are not confined to drought years, because the level is drawn down for generation and for downstream irrigation as well as by the weather. Between the maximum level of 703 m and the minimum operating level of 665 m there is about 38 m of working range. Rainfall over the catchment is lowest in January and highest in October; a Sentinel-1 study of 2017-2022 by Punsisi Rajakaruna, Surajit Ghosh and Bunyod Holmatov found the reservoir's water extent at its smallest in March and largest in August in 2022, 3.63 km2 against 5.41 km2; and a 2017 study of the catchment by Chandrasekara and others in Advances in Meteorology found that although inflow is higher from June to November, in recent decades storage has been drawn down to the dead storage level in August and September, with a falling inflow trend over 1960-2005. Which is to say that the occasion the film needs is real, recurrent and genuinely unforecastable, because it depends on an operating decision as much as on a dry season.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
C074 is a compendium of nine overlapping lists — taints, floods, yokes, knots, clingings, hindrances, latent tendencies, fetters, defilements — and its point is that one small set of mental factors is named nine times over by nine different images. Two of those images are this valley's own engineering. The floods are explained as a current that carries whatever falls into the river down to the floor of the sea, and by the second source as a great mass of water going over fields, gardens and villages, with escape from it very hard. That is not offered here as a resemblance. A programme of works put a measured volume of water over a measured area of fields, gardens and villages, and the record gives the volume, the area, the top level and the day the gates closed. When a film can put a figure on the simile, the simile stops being decoration and becomes a description.

The second image is the one the place answers most exactly, and it needs stating carefully rather than loudly. Among C074's lists are the latent tendencies, which the digest glosses as unwholesome states that lie dormant until a suitable object appears; the sources set out three stages — lying low, surfacing in the mind, and breaking out into speech or act — and only the last of the three can be photographed. A latent tendency is therefore defined by a negative that is hard to show: it is not absent while it is invisible, and nothing about it changes when it becomes visible except the conditions around it. A building standing in mud at the elevation it has always occupied is that shape, and it is that shape without anybody having to assert it. The temple did not rise. The water went down. Its position, its plan and its courses are the same at 665 m as they were at 703 m; the only variable in the whole arrangement is how much was standing over it. That is also why the closing beat matters more than the reveal: the level goes back up, and the digest is explicit that holding something down and being finished with it are two different operations — practice and absorption suppress, only path-knowledge uproots. A reservoir has a word for the first of those and no word at all for the second, so the film can show suppression honestly and must say what it cannot show.

Two limits keep this from being overstated. The digest itself flags that one of the sources says the latent tendencies are neither strictly ultimate realities nor not ultimate realities, calls this doctrinally subtle, notes that the other source does not discuss it, and says it needs expert checking before any on-screen statement. So the film uses the shape of the idea and does not make a claim about its status. And the digest rules out the reading a clean floor under clean water invites: the remark that the life-continuum mind carries no unwholesome factors is a technical statement about one kind of mind-moment and not a claim about a pure self underneath, which the same text rejects. Ground that has kept its edges under water is a fact about lime and brick, not evidence about anybody.

C008 supplies the surface and, unexpectedly, the production problem. Delusion is described as what darkens the mind so a matter cannot be known as it really is, and doubt as a mind unable to reach a decision about its object; both come with neutral feeling, because what has not been grasped can be neither liked nor disliked, and the digest insists that this flatness is dullness and not equanimity. A full reservoir is precisely a surface that withholds: 90 m at its deepest, giving nothing back, and flat at evening without being calm. But C008's second guard is the one that earns this location its honesty. The Pradeepika separates the doubt it means — a stalling over eight specific religious matters — from ordinary uncertainty about something one simply cannot yet find out, and says the second may not be unwholesome at all. Nobody can say when the level will fall far enough. Not the crew, not the authority, not the meteorologists whose own papers disagree about whether the minimum falls in March or in August. That not-knowing is the film's central unknown and it is exactly the kind the source declines to call a defilement, which means the film can be truthful about its own ignorance without turning that ignorance into an exhibit.

The last thing the history does is fix what the film must not do. This is a modern administrative record, not a chronicle with a legend in it, and the people it counted are alive. The concepts here are about mental factors and nothing in either digest licenses a verdict on a scheme, a government or a displaced population; C074's warnings about rites and rituals concern views held as the path to liberation and cannot be turned on anyone who comes to the exposed image house to make an offering. So the record is set down once, with its figures and their disagreements, and left. What the film films is water, mud and masonry.
what_is_certain: The Kotmale Dam is an embankment dam on the Kotmale Oya, the largest right-bank tributary of the Mahaweli Ganga, and was the most upstream of the headworks of the Accelerated Mahaweli Development Programme. It is 87 m high with three spillways.
A dam here was first proposed in 1961; investigations ran 1964-1968 and a feasibility study 1973-1976, the latter by Water Power Development Consultancy Services of India.

Construction began in 1979. Filling of the reservoir began in November 1984, against a contractual completion date of 22 August 1985; the dam was ceremonially completed in February 1985 and generation began in 1985.

The project began as an agreement between two private Swedish contractors and the Sri Lankan government, and the Swedish International Development Authority (SIDA) was brought in during construction because of financial constraints. Lars T. Soeftestad, writing for the Development Studies Unit at the University of Stockholm, states that SIDA's agreeing to provide the funds 'in fact meant "taking over" the implementation of a project designed by others', and that the original agreement left all responsibility for evacuation and relocation with the Sri Lankan government.

Ceylon Electricity Board station data for Kotmale give a maximum reservoir level of 703 m above mean sea level, a minimum level of 665 m, gross storage to top water level of 174 million cubic metres, usable volume 154 million cubic metres, and a catchment of 544 km2. Three vertical Francis units of 67 MW each give 201 MW installed, at a rated 201.5 m effective head, with an expected 450 GWh a year. Water is carried about 7.2 km underground to the power station at Atabage.
At normal top water level the reservoir surface is 6.5 km2, its maximum depth 90 m, mean depth 26.8 m and shoreline 45 km.
The reservoir was renamed the Gamini Dissanayaka Reservoir on 11 April 2003.

The Kotmale Evacuees Study, commissioned by SIDA and begun in the spring of 1988, records 3,056 families already relocated: 1,334 who took relocation higher up the hillsides within the Kotmale valley, and 1,722 who moved downstream and out of Kotmale, with a further 905 families listed for evacuation upstream, making 3,961 in all. Evacuation had two causes, inundation and subsequent landslides. Published by Lars T. Soeftestad in Bistandsantropologen no. 15, pp 22-32, June 1990.

The same study states that no data on the situation prior to evacuation existed, so it could not be conceived as an evaluation and had to be run as an impact analysis; and that the official promise of 0.8 ha of land per family for those relocated within the valley was not kept, actual allotments running between 0.2 and 0.8 ha.

Those relocated downstream went largely into the large settlement schemes of the lower Mahaweli, in the dry zone. A later study by Jagath Manatunge and Naruhiko Takesada, International Journal of Water Resources Development 29(1), 2013, pp 87-100, revisited resettlers at eight sites in Mahaweli Systems B, C and H.
Named religious sites recorded as submerged include the Kadadora Vihara, the Thispane Vihara, the Othalawa Vihara, the Medagoda Vihara, the Morape Devalaya and a Pattini Devalaya.

The temple that reappears is the Kadadora Sri Priyabimbaramaya Viharaya, in Kadadora, Nuwara Eliya district, recorded at 7.06083 N, 80.59722 E. Its described plan is an image house with a garbhagriha containing the principal Buddha figure, smaller rooms and gathering space around it, and wall paintings of scenes from the Buddha's life and the Jataka stories.

The Kotmale Mahaweli Maha Seya was raised in connection with the submerged temples and the people who lost property. It came from a proposal by Gamini Dissanayake, then Minister of Mahaweli Development; its structural design was by Vidya Jyothi Dr A. N. S. Kulasinghe, who died before it was completed; President J. R. Jayewardene laid the foundation stone on 20 March 1983; it is 88 m high, stands at about 950 m above sea level above the right bank, and was completed and opened by President Maithripala Sirisena and Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe on 20 June 2016. It is described as second in height to the Ruwanwelisaya at Anuradhapura.

The ruins have been above water on datable occasions. A Daily News report of 30 March 2016 describes ruins emerging as levels dropped. Photographs on Wikimedia Commons carry camera dates of 23 April 2016, 3 August 2017, 15-19 April 2019 and 5 May 2020. Sinhala press reports appeared in April 2019 and April 2021, and a Sinhala broadcaster reported on 5 February 2026 that the statues were visible again after the level fell rapidly following the rains of Cyclone Ditwah in late November 2025.

The Kotmale reservoir was at or above spill level in early December 2025 and controlled release was begun; two months later the level had fallen far enough to expose the temple. The drawdown is therefore not exclusive to drought years.

Structures recorded as visible when the level is low: the image house and its walls, a seated Buddha figure, carved stone work including a makara torana at the entrance, a bodhigharaya wall, a flower altar, and paintings faintly traceable on remaining plaster. Across the water the Thispane Vihara surfaces, of which only foundation walls remain, and further east a gopuram tower of a former Hindu temple can emerge.

Rainfall over the catchment is lowest in January and highest in October. A Sentinel-1 SAR study of 2017-2022 by Punsisi Rajakaruna, Surajit Ghosh and Bunyod Holmatov reports the reservoir's minimum water extent in March and maximum in August for 2022, at 3.63 km2 and 5.41 km2.

A 2017 study of the catchment by Chandrasekara and others in Advances in Meteorology reports that although inflow is higher from June to November, in recent decades storage has been drawn down to the reservoir's dead storage level during August and September, and that inflow shows a decreasing trend over 1960-2005. The paper's purpose is to use ENSO phase as an input to water management for the reservoir.
what_is_disputed: The month construction began. Accounts give February 1979, August 1979 and September 1979. The year is not in doubt.
The crest length of the dam: 520 m in some accounts, 600 m in others.

The date the reservoir was commissioned. Most accounts give 1985, and one Sinhala feature gives 27 February 1985 as the day the gates were closed; generation is put at early 1985 in one account and June 1985 in another; the Ceylon Electricity Board's own station page gives 1988. These are probably different milestones rather than a contradiction, but no single document reconciling them was found.
The number of villages submerged. The figure in almost universal circulation is 57; one Sinhala feature says over 50. No official list of the 57 was located.

The number of temples and shrines submerged. Around 54 is the commonest figure; the account of the commemorative stupa says over 50; another site says about 50; one Sinhala feature says 18. These are kept apart rather than averaged, and the film does not state a number it cannot source.

The area inundated. Nearly 4,000 ha of the upper catchment, including 600 ha of paddy, is the figure in the water-resources literature; 2,270 ha (5,610 acres) across the Kandy and Nuwara Eliya districts is given as the reservoir's coverage. It is not clear from the sources whether these measure the same thing.

The number of families moved. 3,056 relocated plus 905 listed, making 3,961, is the Kotmale Evacuees Study's own figure; around 3,400 including some 900 from landslide-prone ground appears elsewhere; approximately 3,000 appears in popular accounts. The study itself says there was no baseline data, which is the reason the figures differ.

The reservoir's elevation. 703 m above mean sea level is the Ceylon Electricity Board's figure; one popular account gives 2,100 feet, which is about 640 m. The catchment is given as 544 km2 by the Ceylon Electricity Board, 563 km2 by another site, and 730 square miles in a popular account, which cannot be the same quantity. Installed capacity is 201 MW in the technical sources and 206 MW in one popular account.

The age of the temple. Some accounts identify the site with an ancient temple called Pratibimbarama, the monastery of the reflection, and speak of a history running back several centuries; others state that the building submerged in the 1980s was put up by the villagers in the early twentieth century. The two claims are not necessarily incompatible - an old site can carry a new building - but nothing found here establishes either, and no excavation report or inscription was located. The film does not date the building.

Widely repeated and contradicted: that the ruins have been visible only three or four times in more than thirty years. Dated photographs and press reports place exposures in April 2016, August 2017, April 2019, May 2020, April 2021 and February 2026, which is at least six in eleven years.
Widely repeated, not established: that the site is visible only in March and April. April is the commonest month in the record, but the 2017 exposure is dated to August and the 2026 one to February.

Which month the reservoir is lowest. A satellite study gives the minimum water extent in March; a catchment study reports storage reaching dead storage level in August and September. Surface extent and stored volume are not the same measurement and the studies cover different years, but the two findings point at different months and the film cannot rely on either.

The first reappearance. It is said to have happened around 2009 after roughly thirty years, which counts from the start of construction in 1979 rather than from the submergence in 1985. No report of an exposure between 1985 and 2009 was found, and an absence of reports is not evidence that none occurred.

The claimed connection between the Kotmale valley and Prince Gemunu's flight to Malaya Rata appears in Sri Lankan popular writing about the site. No chronicle passage or scholarly treatment of it was located and the film makes no use of it.

Above all, what none of this settles. The record establishes what the scheme did, when, with what volumes, and how many families were counted as moved. It does not settle whether that was worth doing, for whom, or at whose cost, and nothing in this block is to be read as an answer to those questions or as an account of anyone's loss. Where the figures disagree, that they disagree is the finding.

what_to_film: The full reservoir first, high and wide from the air, so the film establishes a surface that tells the viewer nothing.
The tide line round the whole valley once the level drops: green stopping dead at a level, and a pale band of cracked silt below it.
The exposed street plan from directly overhead in low sun, when every foundation and threshold throws a shadow and the settlement reads as a plan.
Surfaces in close-up at walking speed: plaster that has kept its face, brick courses, a well rim, steps with their edges intact, mud drying into plates.
The metalled road that runs down the slope and continues into the water, filmed from both the land and the air.
The temple platform and its statues, filmed as found, without moving, cleaning or lighting anything, and without adjudicating anybody's practice there.

Across the water, the foundation walls of a second temple that also surfaces, and further east the gopuram tower of a former Hindu temple, if the level is low enough to bring either out. They differentiate the valley from a single-building film and they are recorded in the sources.
The same aerial frames again after the first heavy rain in the catchment, once the water is back, cut hard against the drawdown frames.

The 88 m stupa on the high ground above the right bank only as a fact of the skyline in wide frames, if at all. It was raised in connection with the submergence and the film does not use it as a memorial or let it carry a sentiment the narration refuses.
suggested_location.access: By road from Kandy through Gampola and Ulapane to the Kotmale side, roughly 38 km, then down to whichever shoreline the level has opened; there is a signposted reservoir observation point above the Kadadora arm that is the reliable first stop for judging the level. Access to the exposed bed depends entirely on the drawdown and on the reservoir authority, and the whole film depends on being able to move within days of a level being reached: the February 2026 exposure followed a fall that took about two months from spill level. Because the drawdown is an operating decision as much as a weather event, the Mahaweli Authority and the Ceylon Electricity Board hold the data that would give any warning at all, and a standing enquiry with them is worth more than a weather forecast. Drone work over a dam and its reservoir is infrastructure filming and will need specific permission.
suggested_location.best_time: Whenever the level is low, which is not only in drought years. The reservoir's working range is about 38 m, from a maximum level of 703 m above mean sea level down to a minimum operating level of 665 m, and the dated record of exposures runs April 2016, August 2017, April 2019, May 2020, April 2021 and February 2026 - April commonest, but by no means only. Catchment rainfall is lowest in January and highest in October; one satellite study puts the smallest water surface in March, while a catchment study reports storage reaching dead storage level in August and September, so the two literatures disagree and neither can be planned against. Within a day: early morning for mist and the ridges above the tide line, the last hour of light for the exposed masonry, when low sun makes every wall base throw a shadow.

suggested_location.research_note: Researched properly on 2026-09-25 and a historical_thread added; several earlier figures in this record were corrected. The coordinates are now the ones published for the temple itself, 7.06083 N / 80.59722 E, rounded to four places, replacing an approximate point on the reservoir arm taken from route descriptions; they are still a desk figure and should be fixed on the ground. The dam and reservoir figures - 87 m high, 703 m maximum level, 665 m minimum operating level, 174 million cubic metres gross and 154 usable, 6.5 km2 surface, 544 km2 catchment, 3 x 67 MW - are from the Ceylon Electricity Board's own Mahaweli complex station page and are the most authoritative numbers in the file. The submergence counts (57 villages, 14 estates, around 54 temples) are repeated across popular and encyclopaedic sources and no official list behind them was found; the variants, including one Sinhala feature giving over 50 villages and 18 temples, are kept in what_is_disputed rather than averaged. The resettlement figures come from the Kotmale Evacuees Study as published by Lars T. Soeftestad in 1990, which is the best-sourced account located and which states that no pre-evacuation baseline data existed at all - that absence is why the family counts differ between sources. Two claims previously in this record are now corrected: the site has not surfaced only 'three or four times' or 'a handful of times' in more than thirty years (dated photographs and press reports give April 2016, August 2017, April 2019, May 2020, April 2021 and February 2026), and it is not confined to March and April (the August 2017 and February 2026 exposures rule that out). The February 2026 exposure is the most important single finding for production: it came after the reservoir had been at spill level in early December 2025, which means the drawdown that exposes the temple is an operating decision as much as a drought, and the reservoir authority rather than the weather service is the body to ask. What could not be established: any official list of the submerged settlements; the age of the temple, where the 'ancient Pratibimbarama' identification and the 'built by the villagers in the early twentieth century' account sit side by side in the sources with no excavation report or inscription behind either; whether the wider village fabric of wells, doorsteps and street plan that several beats assume has ever actually been above water; and a single document reconciling the 1985 and 1988 commissioning dates. Access to the exposed bed, its safety, reservoir-authority permission and drone rules over dam infrastructure remain entirely unverified. All seven images were confirmed to exist through the Commons query API and their camera dates and descriptions read; the two general pictures are captioned as general pictures.

unknowns: When the level will next fall far enough. The drawdown is a real and recurrent event - six exposures are on record in eleven years - but it depends on an operating decision as much as on rainfall, so it cannot be forecast from weather alone, and the two published studies of the reservoir's seasonality name different months as the lowest. Whether the reservoir authority would give advance notice of a planned drawdown is the single most valuable thing that could be established before production.

How much of the drowned ground the film can actually show. What the record documents standing out of the water is the temple - its image house, walls, a seated Buddha figure, carved stone and a flower altar - plus the foundation walls of a second temple and a gopuram tower. A wider village fabric of wells, doorsteps and a readable street plan is described nowhere in the sources found, and several beats assume it. This needs checking against footage from a past exposure before the film is committed to.
Whether the exposed bed can be walked safely, and how close a crew may get to the structures, is unverified.
Permission to fly a drone over a dam and its reservoir is unverified and may be refused outright.

Whether filming at the exposed temple would interfere with anyone's observance there has not been checked. The reports describe large crowds arriving daily during an exposure, which is a consent problem as well as a logistical one.
